name: Calories and nutrition
summary: Record your food, understand what is in it and keep the history — three jobs a food diary has to handle without extra work.
lead:
Yesterday’s soup, half a casserole, coffee on the run — food rarely matches a tidy portion out of a catalog. First a person needs to record what they actually ate. If every lunch turns into a search and a recalculation, even detailed statistics stay empty.

After that the jobs diverge. One person only needs to repeat the usual dishes, another needs particular nutrients, a third needs entries for a conversation with a specialist. What follows traces that path from fast entry to a history that can still be used months later.

audiencesArt.alt: Different jobs in the “Calories and nutrition” category.

audiences.title: Logging the usual diet
audiences.body: With a settled diet it matters more to repeat the familiar than to search from scratch every time. The person has already put time into their own foods and dishes. What they need is short daily entry with the option to change the portion or a single ingredient while keeping the rest of the record.

audiences.title: Accounting for home cooking and the real portion
audiences.body: A home cook knows what went into the whole batch but eats only part of it. They need to link the recipe to the portion, choose a familiar unit of measure and correct the amount later. The same name for a dish, meanwhile, can hide different ingredients.

audiences.title: Watching food for your own purpose
audiences.body: Some people watch particular nutrients, others gather a history for a conversation with a specialist. These jobs are different from counting a total for the day. It helps to choose the information you need and to see where it came from, without filling the screen with every figure available.

sections.title: First — record your food
sections.intro: The most frequent operation has to account for familiar foods, home recipes and the chance of getting the portion wrong.

observations.title: A familiar breakfast — without a new search
passages: A repeating breakfast turns the diary into a short ritual: pick your own entry, adjust the amount, save. After the initial work of setting up recipes and foods, that saving is especially noticeable. A personal database should make the next entry easier, not merely pile up in the calendar.

Copying a meal helps keep the usual composition. If one yogurt or the size of the portion has changed today, it has to be possible to correct exactly that. A reminder can round out such a ritual, but it must not get in the way of recording food quickly.

Search has to take personal history into account too. If a person always picks one flavor of a product, five other options ahead of it create extra work. Recent and saved items are worth telling apart and showing before similar results from the general database.

quotes.text: I like this app. Especially once I got all my recipes and foods I eat in there, super quick!

So excited that RP came out with an amazing app to help keep track each day. I found it very user friendly and love that I can duplicate meals since I eat the same thing most days. The reminders "time to eat" is so helpful since I live such a busy lifestyle...it helps me space out my food appropriately.

My number one pet peeve is the search function. It is beyond me why when I start to type in a food, the suggestions that come up are not foods that I have saved or logged recently. It is maddening. For example, when I type in Premier Protein, it brings up 5 flavors ahead of the flavor I use on a reg

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “A familiar breakfast — without a new search”.

observations.title: Recognize it, and let it be corrected
passages: A photo of the plate cuts out the search for individual components, and a barcode helps find a packaged product. The two methods rest on different grounds: an image has to be interpreted, a code matched against a catalog record. In both cases the person needs to see exactly what is about to land in the diary.

Show the name, the composition and the amount before saving. For packaging, a check against the label is convenient; for a dish, correcting the components and the portion. Good fast entry includes a short path to an edit: having noticed a mistake, the person carries on with the entry instead of starting the food search from an empty screen.

The value of speed is easy to measure wrongly here. A card filled in instantly does not yet mean a finished entry: the person may spend a minute correcting the wrong composition. The more meaningful question is how many actions are left before saving food they themselves recognize on the screen.

quotes.text: I love this app. Calorie counting is simple. Take a picture of my plate, and the app figures calories for the entire meal. No more looking up each individual food. I also love the hydration portion.
Finally committed to tracking my Marcos using an app rather than eye balling it and this app has made it beyond easy!! The bar code scanner is a cheat code forsure.
The AI called chicken potato chips. It said a 60 calorie low carb tortilla was over 2000 calories.

observations.title: Finding food from your own kitchen
passages: A large database does not solve the job if the usual home-cooked food, a local product or a particular item from a menu is hard to find in it. A similar name does not always do either: the composition and the size can differ. Convenience then depends on how easy it is to create your own entry and use it again.

Tie the search to personal additions and keep the option that was chosen. For a new item it helps to tell apart the information from the packaging, the composition of a recipe and an estimate entered by the person. That makes it possible to refine the entry later and to understand where a number came from, without turning every lunch into filling in a reference book all over again.

A personal recipe can close a gap in a large database. But for that, the dish that was added has to be findable under its usual name and to stay available after a change of phone. For a first product, a narrow library of one cuisine may turn out to be more useful than a huge catalog in which a matching entry is hard to tell from an approximate one.

quotes.text: This app gives very few options for foods for a home cook. I do not eat out often. I also cook from scratch. I just quit My Fitness Pal. It appears this app will not suffice my as well.

I get it, the app is good for American users or ones who eat mostly packaged meals. But if you are living abroad and homecoming a variety of meals, it's hard to use. Wish there was a larger base of users with similar eating habits.

I tried to add a simple item, the Chick-fil-A grilled patty and it wasn't an option. When I searched for it in the AI, it returned no results. When you are trying to count macros having the flexibility to add detailed items is crucial.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Finding food from your own kitchen”.

observations.title: Separating what was cooked from what was eaten
passages: A recipe describes the whole of what was cooked, the diary entry the part that was eaten. When those levels are mixed, the ingredients have to be entered all over again. The overall composition, the cooked weight or the number of servings should be kept with the dish, while the amount eaten is chosen when it is added to a day.

When cooking for several days, a dish created once can be used again. A change to the next batch must not quietly rewrite past portions. That keeps the history meaningful even if the composition of a familiar casserole shifts over time.

Units of entry are a separate question. A person may weigh oil in grams while the app asks for milliliters. It has to show which quantity is expected and support suitable ways of recording it without a hidden conversion. A menu and the use of leftovers are a possible continuation of this job, one that is developed in the next idea.

quotes.text: The app can be a great tool if you're eating chicken and rice everyday because you can measure those out one at a time. Where it struggled for me is if you're trying to make a meal prep recipe for the week. There's nowhere to create a recipe, add in how many servings or the total weight, and then add it to a day.

Finally committed to tracking my Marcos using an app rather than eye balling it and this app has made it beyond easy!! The bar code scanner is a cheat code forsure and it's relatively easy to build and create new meals if you are meal prepping.

I have two issues with this app: I can enter my weight only in pounds. I want to use kg. There should be an option to choose. I don't measure my olive oil in ml, I just want to be able to put in weight in grams.

placements.title: Separating what was cooked from what was eaten

sections.title: Counting what the person needs
sections.intro: The same entries can be used for different purposes. The purpose decides what is worth putting on the first screen.

observations.title: Take the goal into account instead of imposing it
passages: A diary can serve different purposes. One review values watching weight and the calculated continuation of the chart. It matters to tell measurements already entered apart from a forecast, and the goal the person has chosen apart from the app’s automatic assumption.

Another author praises having calories and macros changed on the basis of the diary. That is a personal assessment, not proof that the app determines metabolism accurately. When a target changes, the previous value, the grounds for the revision and a way to see the underlying entries are all needed.

A mismatch of purpose is especially visible when a person expects to gain and the app keeps lowering the targets. A complaint like that cannot be closed with a new chart. The suggestion has to be kept apart from the user’s decision and from a plan agreed with a specialist. A diary with no calculated goals remains a separate alternative — the card below looks at it.

quotes.text: I absolutely love this app. I have been using it for many years now. It does exactly what I want to do. One thing I love about it: I am able to detect patterns in weight loss and weight gain. I also love the prediction algorithms. I can see a predicted weight on a date based on a predicted weight goal.

This app is truly designed for real life. The adaptive calorie and macro adjustments based on your metabolism just makes sense. Tracking your macros/calories alongside your daily weight makes so much more sense than tracking movement or activity. All the trackers and estimates of caloric output is just noise.

Easy to track Macros and yes for the most part it absolutely helps you lose weight but as far as building muscle it really doesn't because it gives you less and less calories each time less protein, less carbs, I'm currently at 1200 calories and I'm always hungry.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Take the goal into account instead of imposing it”.

placements.title: Take the goal into account instead of imposing it

observations.title: Tell a gap in the data from a zero
passages: Total calories answer only one question. A particular diary may need protein, fiber or selected vitamins and minerals. A detailed screen, though, is only as useful as the data filled in about the food that was logged. A missing value and a real zero cannot be shown the same way.

Let people choose the main figures and open the details for a food. Mark the gaps in the summary, so that it is clear which entries need refining. This approach helps prepare substantive questions about your own diet and does not overload daily entry with figures the person does not use.

A fiber total, for instance, says little if that field is empty for half of the foods logged. Next to the total it helps to explain that the calculation is incomplete and to allow particular items to be refined. Recording targets set by a specialist is also different from the app assigning targets itself.

quotes.text: I've used this app for ~6 years with varied consistency, different goals, diets, and hrt. It's probably the MOST comprehensive and customizable FREE fitness+nutrition tracker. What initially stood out to me was micronutrient tracking which idk any free app that does (or even paid!).

The psychology is good but the biggest place where Noom is failing its paid subscribers is there is no fiber tracking. In 2026 when fiber & protein are what we are being told is most important, we can't track both with a $200 subscription? When so many of us are on GLP-1s?

I actually really like this app. Being able to input foods and accurately track my macros helps me stay on track. My qualm is where is the fiber tracker? We are focusing more on overall wellness than ever before.

sections.title: Coming back to the data and carrying on
sections.intro: Over time the value of a diary moves from individual numbers to the work built up in it: the recipes, the observations and a familiar way of entering things.

observations.title: Build a history that can be checked against the source
passages: Looking at food, weight and activity together can cut down on switching between diaries. One positive review values the trainer’s feedback as well. But joining sources is only useful when it is clear which data was actually transferred.

A missed measurement and a day without a measurement are different cases. When weight comes across rarely, show the last record received and its source, so that the person can check a day they remember against the original app.

Duplication creates the opposite error: one activity is represented several times. In the last review that affects the subsequent calculation as well. Before merging, rules for recognizing repeats and access to the original events are needed. A combined chart must not hide which entries its total is made of.

quotes.text: I've been enjoying this app and its ease of use! It fully integrates with my training app and allows my fitness trainer to provide regular feedback!

I like using this app it takes the effort out of monitoring my exercise, and calorie intake. However, I have linked it to Apple health and it has only retrieved my weight four times in about two months! I'm sure this is an easy fix.
Pulls exercise from Apple Health. Steps, walking, elliptical are all added to your total steps. Gives false reading for how many calories you can take in because exercise is double counted.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Build a history that can be checked against the source”.

placements.title: Build a history that can be checked against the source
placements.body: Once the entries are gathered, different ways of using them appear: set food next to a measurement, prepare your own history for an appointment, or open a chosen period to a specialist. These are separate scenarios, not three names for one integration.

observations.title: Keep the recipes and the familiar way of logging
passages: A personal database is not only daily totals. It includes the foods someone created, complex recipes, the names of meals and the favorites. It is this prepared part that makes it possible to come back after a break and carry on quickly. Losing it means doing the work again, even when the weight chart has survived.

When transferring and restoring, show what the available data consists of. It helps to open your own recipe, check the ingredients and add it to a new day. That check reveals more than a message about an archive having uploaded successfully: it becomes clear whether what was built up can really be used.

Coming back after a break is a product scenario of its own. Yesterday’s diary may be empty while the favorite dishes are still useful. If a person opens a familiar recipe and logs lunch in a few actions, the database they have built is already working for them, with no demand to restore every missed day.

quotes.text: I am done with this app. It IS great, tracks my protein and carb intake very well. But for the third time I have lost all of my previous numbers, custom foods, all my statistics. I know it's free, but if I have to KEEP entering food information every time this randomly erases all of my info, it's not worth it.

Great when it works, but twice now it has crashed or been offline for days "for major improvements" that never materialize. The worst part of this is that ALL your stored data (including the recipes you've laboriously built and saved) is erased!

I used to use this app regularly and had all of my meals named with my macro goals for that meal and a bunch of favorite foods. Now I come back to the app after a few months not counting and discover you've wiped ALL of that away and ruined all the effort I put into this app previously.

conclusion.title: Start with repeatable entry of your own food
conclusion.body:
Start by testing a week of the usual diet: whether your own foods can be found, whether dishes copy across, whether the portions are clear and whether a mistake is easy to fix. This is where a diary either saves daily effort or keeps demanding that the food be described from scratch. A more detailed report does not make up for missed and approximate entries.

Then choose what the history is being read for. Repeating a familiar menu, reviewing particular nutrients, a photo diary and preparing for an appointment call for different screens and different data. They can be developed separately. The priority is a clear origin for the entries and the ability to manage them; an automatic change of targets should not be passed off as a confirmed understanding of what the body needs.
